# 08-fresco — sources

Back-test entry `08-fresco.yaml`: Fresco, the AI scribe for construction superintendents (YC Fall 2024).
Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim from the page named; "Author's choice" marks the
smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent.

Main sources:
- [HN] Launch HN: Fresco (YC F24), 2024-11-21 — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42204939
- [LYC] Launch YC: Fresco, the scribe for construction, 2024-10-23 — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/M73-fresco-the-scribe-for-construction
- [YCP] YC company page — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/fresco (now "AI-powered takeoff and estimating for Division 8 construction")
- [KOE] A contractor's daily-log expectations on Procore's support site — https://support.procore.com/tc/Koester/Site_Map/Koester_Expectations_-_Daily_Logs
- [SWI] Swiftask, Procore daily reports page (vendor) — https://swiftask.ai/ai-integration/procore/intelligent-daily-reports
- [BLS] BLS Occupational Outlook, construction managers — https://www.bls.gov/ooh/management/construction-managers.htm
- [OPU] Launch HN: Opusense (field reports for site inspectors), 2025-05-20 — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44042791

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Construction superintendents on commercial jobs.
   [HN] "Superintendents are the busiest and most expensive people on construction sites."
   [LYC] "That’s the reality for 210k+ construction superintendents (or supervisors, foremen, PMs, etc.) across the USA."
   → `roles[superintendent]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`. Author's choice: "on commercial jobs" (the founders ask
   for introductions to commercial general contractors in [LYC]).

2. **What (the job).** Keep the record of the day's work, for liability and disputes.
   [HN] "30-200 photos per day to document site progress (mostly for liability reasons, or in case of a dispute with the
   owner over delays and deliverables)"; photos used to create "daily logs", "structured documents that account for the
   work done on site on any given day". [KOE] the log is "a critical piece of documentation in the arbitration of a
   dispute". → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At the end of the day, after the site walks, in the trailer.
   [HN] "At the end of the day, they'll spend a few hours uploading those photos into OneDrive, or project management
   software like Procore or ACC." [YCP] "We were curious what superintendents were doing for hours in their trailers at
   the end of the day." [LYC] "supes are spending up to 3 hours a day creating documents". → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: daily log`.
   Author's choice: the recall window {5, WORKING_DAYS} and Frequency 4 to 5 working days out of 5 (the posts say "per
   day"; a five-day site week is assumed). Prevalence `p_80_100` ("Nearly all") follows from the same "per day".

4. **Which people (the comparable group).** Superintendents at US general contractors whose jobs run on Procore or ACC.
   [LYC] "210k+ construction superintendents ... across the USA"; "Project management tools like Procore and ACC have
   dramatically increased documentation requirements". [YCP] "driving to Napa, South Bay, and around SF". → `context.segment`,
   `market: US`.

5. **Who pays.** The general contractor, per site.
   [HN] "we charge per site per month, which includes unlimited users on any given construction project".
   → `persona.decision_maker: {role: contractor}`, the BUYER role. Author's choice: the decider is the contractor's
   "operations lead" and the role to test is "The CFO" (a second role, "The project executive", listed); Purchase
   friction's three steps ("A trial on one live job" tested, a Procore check, a security review) and Commitment's step
   "start a paid pilot on one site" are the author's. Public material names no buyer title; [LYC] asks for
   introductions to general contractors by firm, not by role.

6. **Mechanism.** Narrated short videos turned into notes, texted to the crew, pushed to Procore/ACC.
   [HN] "Supers simply take short videos with voiceover, or upload photos, and Fresco does the rest, creating notes with
   transcription, photos, assignees, and due dates. Supers can easily text their crew action items, and receive texts
   back". "We also route this to whatever project management software they're using with a single click."
   [LYC] the narrated example "The beam in the southwest corner of room 134 is corroded and needs replacement by Alex.";
   "Supes who use Fresco complete their notes, on average, 90% faster."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, Compatibility and Adoption friction items. Relative advantage's two
   benefits are from [HN] ("during their site walks, not after") and [LYC] ("90% faster"); their wording is the author's.

7. **Price.** About $1k per site per month, less with multi-site or multi-month terms.
   [HN] "The typical price is $1k/month, but we offer discounts for multi-month or multi-site commitments."
   → `commercial.price` {800, 1000, month}. Author's choice: the low end of $800 stands for the stated discounts.
   Existing sacrifice: 30 to 60 hours a month per site at an hourly rate of 55 — from [LYC] "up to 3 hours a day" and
   [HN] "a few hours uploading", taken as 1.5 to 3 hours on about twenty working days (author's arithmetic). The rate is
   [BLS] "$55.28 per hour" (median, construction managers, May 2025), the author's stand-in: no superintendent wage is
   in the public material. Ability to pay is derived by code (24% to 61%).

8. **Occasions.** The narrated beam; a school refit report; the uploads and logs at the end of the day.
   [LYC] on a school refit walkthrough: "Normally, creating the final report takes 2+ hours."
   [HN] "few supers have time to do this thoroughly, so these photos aren't very searchable." No named customer quote
   exists in public; the occasions below are scripted from these and from practitioner comments.

No respondent carries the name of a commenter, customer or founder.

## Open
- The verdict was scripted to be plausible and not obviously "build": the problem holds on how often but people
  disagree on whether the log is one of their two worst difficulties; the solution splits on the benefit and on
  talking over videos on site; the price fails (two of eight at the founder's band or above) while the cost it would
  replace is above the price. This is the author's reading of the thread's sceptics, not a measured result.
- No public account names a buyer title at a general contractor; the decider, the tested role "The CFO", the purchase
  steps and the Commitment step are the author's.
- hourly_rate 55 is a proxy (construction managers, not superintendents).
- Existing sacrifice picks use `period: quarter` (the corpus's convention), although the registry's recall period for a
  monthly cost reads "last month"; the values are the monthly figures times three.
- The window {5, WORKING_DAYS} is the author's; the public posts say "per day".

founder.order_why: The flow runs sensibly from context to problem to fielding, but screen 4 (how recent an episode must be) splits the two identical-looking context screens 3 and 5, and I'd rather set the recall window after the context is fully defined.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 carry the same question ('Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies'); screens 8 and 9 feel close, though one asks how many supers and the other how many days, so they are not true repeats.
founder.missing: Nothing on the solution, the price or who pays, even though the study's verdict depends on them: narrated site videos turned into notes pushed to Procore/ACC, about $1k per site per month, and the general contractor as buyer rather than the superintendent answering. screens.why1: After choosing how they answer, the last thing before sending is who receives it, so the question is obvious here, though the kicker says SENT when I haven't sent anything yet.
screens.why2: "Who gets a link?" reads at once and each option explains itself in a line, with only "the Contacts page" pointing at a part of Keel I may not have opened yet.
screens.why3: I know whether I'm texting supers I met driving around Napa and the South Bay, working from a list, or posting in a group, so I can answer from what I actually do.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover how I would reach superintendents, and my real answer, people I know by name, is right there with no escape chip needed.
screens.why5: The screen keeps my pick of people by name and adds no wording that changes my study, my superintendents or my product.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 7 said yes", and with my bar of 8 in 10 just below it I can see that the count decides the verdict, though I have to do the sum myself.
screens.why_b2: It plainly counts people saying yes and shows the bar, but it plots 6 of 7 on a 0-to-10 "in 10" scale, so I need a second look to see that 6 of 7 is about 8.6 in 10 and clears the bar.
screens.why_b3: The question about spending hours typing up the daily log is my problem, but the belief line only says "had this", never says what "this" is, and isn't one of the two lines I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: It says nothing about what this means for Fresco or what I should do next, such as whether how often this happens is settled while the stage as a whole remains uncalled.
screens.why_b5: The n is visible and the claim stays with "these" superintendents, but "Holding up" carries no low-n warning on 7 people when the stage page says "Too few to call", and the seventh person, the only no, is missing from the list.
screens.instead: Holding up, on only 7 people: 6 of 7 (about 8.6 in 10) spent hours typing up the daily log in the last 5 working days, above your 8 in 10; this shows how common it is, not how much it matters, so get more answers before you rely on it, and see the one who said no below.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits directly beside the number that decides it, '4 answered · 5 needed to call it', so I know there is no answer yet and exactly why.
screens.why_b2: The working-days axis, the 4-to-5 bar and the middle answer of 5 are plain, but I need a second look to square 4 answered with six names and to work out 'beyond, the good side' on a scale that stops at 5.
screens.why_b3: The 4-to-5 days out of 5 is my number, but 'face this' doesn't name the daily log, and the question narrows it to 'spend hours typing up', so it is recognisable but reworded.
screens.why_b4: '5 needed to call it' implies I need one more usable answer, but the screen doesn't say so or say what these four answers mean for the idea.
screens.why_b5: It refuses to call the belief on 4 answers, keeps n visible and marks the guess and the refusal as not counted, so it claims nothing beyond the people who answered.
screens.instead: Too few to call: all 4 clear answers put the daily log on 4 to 5 days out of 5, but Hank declined and Luis's answer was a guess, so get one more clear answer from a superintendent before treating frequency as settled.

screens.why_b1: The verdict "Too few to call" sits directly beside the number that decides it, "4 answered · 5 needed to call it", so I know there is no answer yet and why.
screens.why_b2: It takes a second look to see that the bars add to 8 because 4 people each picked two, which the "which one" question hides, and the 2-in-3 bar isn't drawn or stated, so "You said" only marks my option.
screens.why_b3: The name Importance and the belief line are word for word what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The screen doesn't say what to do, such as getting one more usable answer or what 2 of 4 with schedule and subs ahead of the log might mean for the idea.
screens.why_b5: It makes no claim beyond the people who answered, says plainly that 4 is too few, and shows who wasn't counted and why, including a guess and a refusal.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 2 of 4 put the log in their two, and it needs at least 2 in 3 of 5 or more; schedule and subs each got 3, so get one more countable answer before leaning on the log as a top pain, and each bar counts people who picked it in their two.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside the number that decides it, '4 answered · 5 needed to call it', so I know no answer exists yet and exactly why.
screens.why_b2: The bars and the count of 4 are plain, but the line 'You said their way of getting the day into the log.' never shows where my bar of 2 in 3 below 'Done in the trailer in under an hour' sits, so I have to work out that 3 of 4 land below it.
screens.why_b3: The title and the belief line are word for word what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what to do next; I am not told to get more superintendents to answer, how many more, or what this leaves open for the idea.
screens.why_b5: It refuses to call the belief on 4 answers, says the n outright, marks Hank and Luis as not counted, and makes no claim about superintendents in general.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 4 counted, 5 needed. 3 of the 4 land below 'Done in the trailer in under an hour' (your bar: 2 in 3), but one more usable answer is needed before this counts, so get another superintendent to tell you about their last daily log.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Too few to call' is stated on each line, but the number behind it (4 answered, 5 needed) is not on this screen, only group counts of 2 and 1.
screens.why_b3: Importance and Current solution are the dimensions I checked, but my belief lines are gone and only the headings 'why other things come first' and 'what makes today's way work' point back to them.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what this means for the idea or what to do next, such as getting more superintendents to answer or asking how Denise's tablet routine works.
screens.why_b5: It claims nothing beyond the people who answered: 'Too few to call' sits on each line, the counts of 2 and 1 are visible, and the quotes are attributed by name and marked against.
screens.why_b6: I typed about logging photos and notes, and this adds that schedule slips and subs not showing up outrank the log, that 'the log can wait till morning, the deck can't', and that one super finishes on a tablet before leaving the gate, though the same Denise quote appearing twice makes it thin.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 4 of the 5 superintendents needed answered, so this is no verdict yet; the two who ranked other things first named schedule and subs, and one finishes the log on a tablet on site, so get more answers and ask whether the log only matters when a dispute comes.

screens.why1: It's the first thing asked and it's obvious why: they want to know if I'm on the kind of job they're studying before going further.
screens.why2: Procore and ACC are everyday names on my jobs, so I get this on one read or one hearing, though 'run on' is loose but clear enough.
screens.why3: I know exactly what platform my current job is on because I upload to it every day.
screens.why4: Yes and No are clean and a gate needs no escape, but a super between jobs or on a job using both or a different platform has to squeeze into No, and 'running now' misses someone who just finished one.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's Procore-or-ACC segment and tells me nothing about any product or plan.
screens.why6: It's short, one question, and 'ACC' says fine as letters to anyone in my trade; 'I'll read 2 options' is a little stiff for a yes or no but easy to hold.

screens.why1: Once you've asked if my job runs on Procore or ACC, it's an obvious next step to ask about my daily log, and that's who this study is for.
screens.why2: Daily log is my everyday word, but "hours" leaves me unsure whether it means hours on one log or added up over the week, and I'd have to stop and pick one.
screens.why3: I do the daily log every working day, so I can answer this about my own last week, though the time mostly goes on getting photos and notes in, not just typing.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but the bar is set at "hours", so a log I did in 40 minutes gets a flat No, and the two chips are too many, with "one particular daily log" not matching a question about the whole week.
screens.why5: Nothing of anyone's product reaches me, but getting the day's photos and notes into the log has narrowed to "typing up", and "hours" puts the pain in the question before I've said it.
screens.why6: It's one short question ending in "Yes or no", easy to hear once and answer, and no escape is spoken, which is right for a gate.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did you put the day's photos and notes into your daily log yourself? Yes or No.

screens.why1: I just said yes to spending hours on the log last week, so asking how many days that happened is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: I understand it first time, but "hours typing up" is a little off because my log time goes to uploading photos and filling in Procore as much as typing, and "hours" leaves me unsure whether 45 minutes counts.
screens.why3: I do the log every working day and can count last week's bad days from memory or from the log dates.
screens.why4: One through five covers every possible answer after a yes on the screen before, the numbers are distinct, and "I can't recall" fits a question about last week.
screens.why5: It stays on keeping the daily log after the walks are done, and nothing about anyone's product or plan reaches me.
screens.why6: It is one short question with five single numbers that are easy to hold when heard, followed by one short escape.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, on how many days did your daily log, with the photos and notes, take you hours to finish? 1; 2; 3; 4; or 5. Or say I can't recall.

screens.why1: After asking how often the daily log ate my hours, it makes sense to ask how that chore stacks up against the rest of my week.
screens.why2: RFIs, submittals and subs are everyday words on my job, so I get it on first read.
screens.why3: These are the things I actually dealt with last week, so I can pick one straight from memory.
screens.why4: All five are real parts of my job and None of these fits, but keeping the job on schedule overlaps with chasing RFIs and getting subs to show up, since those are what drive the schedule.
screens.why5: It keeps the idea of getting the day's photos and notes into the log, sits it among my other headaches without pushing it, and no product or pitch reaches me.
screens.why6: It is one short question with five short options I can hold when I hear them, and the only thing a voice has to manage is saying RFIs letter by letter, which we do anyway.
screens.instead: Think of your last week on site. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Chasing RFIs and submittals; Updating the schedule; Logging the day's photos and notes; Running safety checks; or Getting subs to show up and finish. Or say None of these.

screens.why1: After asking how often the log eats hours and what I'd want made easier, asking how my last log actually went is the obvious close to this part.
screens.why2: Daily log, the walk and the trailer are all my everyday words, and I can answer on first hearing, though 'getting the day into the log' is a touch soft.
screens.why3: I write the daily log every day, so I know exactly where and when the last one got done.
screens.why4: The options cover my real cases and the escape fits, but where, how long and when are mixed, so a log done in the trailer in two hours after the walk fits two options, and 'Log done on site' overlaps since the trailer is on site.
screens.why5: It stays on getting the day's work into the log after the walks, and nothing of anyone's product or plan reaches me.
screens.why6: It is short and the five options can be held, but the stem is two sentences and 'Log done on site' sounds clipped and out of step with the other options when read aloud.
screens.instead: Think of your last daily log. Where did it get finished? Out on the site during the day; in the trailer that same day; at home that night; the next morning; or it never got written up properly. Or say I can't recall.
